title: Navaratri (nine nights, nine forms; Durga)
hook: the gods pour their light into one form, and she rides out to meet the buffalo demon; then nine nights, nine faces

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holi in the morning: Krishna, Radha, and a pinch of color to close a distance. Did the color come back to you? Today, nine nights in a row. Day one hundred forty-three.

There's a demon with the head of a buffalo, and he can't be beaten. His name is Mahishasura. He has a boon that no man and no god can kill him, and he's used it to throw the gods out of heaven. They come together, furious and helpless. And the story says their anger turns into light. Out of Vishnu, out of Shiva, out of Brahma, out of every god, a blaze pours out, and all of it gathers into one form. She has many arms. Each god hands her a weapon. She rides a lion. And she laughs. Her name is Durga, and today we meet her nine faces.
screen: `A DEMON NO GOD CAN KILL.` → `THE GODS' LIGHT BECOMES ONE FORM.` → `SHE RIDES A LION.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess, a Sanskrit text of seven hundred verses that sits inside the Markandeya Purana. Durga fights the buffalo demon, and he keeps changing shape: a buffalo, a lion, a man with a sword, an elephant, the buffalo again. She meets every shape. In the end she pins him down and he's defeated. Many families say that battle took nine nights, and on the tenth day she won. That's where the festival gets its name. Nava, nine. Ratri, night. Navaratri. And here's the part that makes it a practice. Across the nine nights, many Hindus honor the Goddess in nine forms, one a night, called the Navadurga. She begins as Shailaputri, the daughter of the mountain. Then Brahmacharini, the young woman doing hard discipline. Then Chandraghanta, with a half-moon like a bell on her forehead. Kushmanda, who smiled the universe into being. Skandamata, mother of the war god Skanda. Katyayani, the warrior. Kalaratri, the dark night, fierce and frightening. Mahagauri, shining and calm. And Siddhidatri, the one who gives perfection. Nine faces: a daughter, a student, a warrior, a mother, the darkness itself, and then peace. Traditions differ on the details and the order, and some regions honor other forms. But the idea holds: the same power shows up differently on different nights. Some nights it's gentle. Some nights it's fierce. Both are her. And there's a surprise for those who wait: Navaratri comes twice a year, in spring and in autumn. The autumn one is the big one most people know.
screen: `THE DEMON KEEPS CHANGING SHAPE.` · `NAVA, NINE. RATRI, NIGHT.` · `NINE FORMS, ONE EACH NIGHT.` · `GENTLE OR FIERCE, BOTH ARE HER.` · then, large: `THE SAME POWER, NINE FACES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your face for tonight. Settle, and breathe. Durga shows up as whatever the night needs. So ask: what does today need from me? Maybe the daughter of the mountain: steady, rooted. Maybe the student: disciplined, one more page. Maybe the warrior: say the hard thing. Maybe the mother: gentle with someone small. Maybe just the calm one. Don't overthink it. Let one face come. Then breathe as that face for a while, and notice how it sits in your shoulders. The bell holds the time.
Navaratri. Nine nights. The Goddess in nine forms, one a night, and on the tenth day she wins.
Your line: Navaratri, nine nights, nine forms, Durga. Today, pick the face the day needs, gentle or fierce, and wear it on purpose. Day one hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: During Navaratri many Hindus honor the Goddess in nine forms, the Navadurga, one each night, with fasting, prayers and readings of the Devi Mahatmya; the tenth day, Vijayadashami or Dussehra, celebrates victory.

original.note: Sanskrit: nava, nine, and ratri, night.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nine-day holiday about a goddess.
what it means: nine nights, nine forms of the Goddess, one a night: daughter, student, warrior, mother, the dark night, and peace.
what a scholar hears: the Devi Mahatmya, seven hundred verses inside the Markandeya Purana, the text many Hindus recite during these nights.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya (Markandeya Purana), chapters 2–3: Durga's birth from the gods' radiance and the slaying of Mahishasura
Navadurga (the nine forms honored across Navaratri)

notes: Devi Mahatmya: 'seven hundred verses' (Durga Saptashati); chapters 81–93 of the Markandeya Purana. Confirm.
Mahishasura's shape-changes (buffalo, lion, man with sword, elephant, buffalo) follow Devi Mahatmya ch. 3. Confirm order.
The boon: commonly told as 'no man or god can kill him' (so a woman/goddess does); the Devi Mahatmya itself does not stress the boon. Framed as the story told. Confirm.
'The battle took nine nights' is a popular framing, attributed to 'many families'. Confirm.

Navadurga order and one-line glosses (Shailaputri, Brahmacharini, Chandraghanta, Kushmanda, Skandamata, Katyayani, Kalaratri, Mahagauri, Siddhidatri) follow the common list (e.g. Devi Kavacham). Confirm.
Chaitra (spring) and Sharad (autumn) Navaratri; there are also two lesser 'gupta' Navaratris. Mentioned as 'twice a year'. Confirm.
